documents.unit: Office of the Provost (University Academic Regulations)
documents.title: Code of Academic Integrity (University Academic Regulations, Bulletin 2026-2027)
documents.stance_why: The only AI text defines misuse as 'circumvent learning goals' or research misconduct and says 'What constitutes use or misuse of AI will differ depending on context and discipline'. It sets no default of permit or ban, and refers to a 'written "Course AI Policy"' that instructors write, so the decision is left to courses, i.e. delegates.
documents.summary: The University of Portland bulletin's Code of Academic Integrity lists 'Misuse of AI' beside cheating, forgery and plagiarism. It names three example violations and says what counts differs by context and discipline. It sets no AI stance itself; faculty supply their written Course AI Policy when reporting a violation through the general four-level penalty and procedure system.

units.why: The sentence classes AI misuse as an integrity violation 'comparable to cheating or plagiarism', which is the P36 move of treating improper AI use as misconduct; it binds everyone in the community, so actor is all.
units.anchor: considered a violation of academic integrity comparable to cheating or plagiarism
units.frag_start: The misuse of artificial intelligence
units.policy: The misuse of AI to circumvent learning goals or to engage in research misconduct is considered a violation of academic integrity comparable to cheating or plagiarism.

units.why: The phrase 'circumvent learning goals' gives the reason AI misuse is wrong: it defeats the learning the work is for. This is a skill-building rationale (P41), though stated only as part of the definition of misuse, so I note the partial fit.
units.anchor: to circumvent learning goals
units.frag_start: The misuse of artificial intelligence
units.policy: AI misuse includes using AI technologies to circumvent learning goals.
units.fit_note: Learning is named only as the thing misuse circumvents; no argument about skill-building is developed.

units.why: 'or to engage in research misconduct' extends the AI misuse rule to research, which P62 covers (AI rules for research and scholarship); no venue or funder rules are named, so the fit is partial.
units.anchor: or to engage in research misconduct
units.frag_start: The misuse of artificial intelligence
units.policy: Using AI technologies to engage in research misconduct is a violation of academic integrity.
units.fit_note: Only classes AI-enabled research misconduct as an integrity violation; says nothing about theses, manuscripts, or venue rules.

units.why: The sentence says use and misuse 'will differ depending on context and discipline', so what counts is not fixed centrally. That is the decide-by-context stance, P04; no instructor is explicitly empowered, so the fit is partial.
units.anchor: will differ depending on context and discipline
units.frag_start: What constitutes use or misuse of AI
units.policy: What constitutes use or misuse of AI differs depending on context and discipline.
units.fit_note: Context and discipline, not named instructors, decide; no one is explicitly empowered.

units.why: Item [1] makes 'submitting work generated by AI as one's own without proper acknowledgement' a violation. The wrongdoing is defined by missing acknowledgement, so this is a disclosure rule (P24) rather than P19, which would ban AI-produced work outright.
units.anchor: submitting work generated by AI as one’s own without proper acknowledgement
units.frag_start: submitting work generated by AI
units.fit_note: Also makes passing off AI work as one's own a violation; the text does not say whether acknowledged AI work is acceptable.

units.why: Item [2] makes 'accessing or using AI tools without authorization' a violation, so AI use needs authorization; this is the fallback rule that unauthorized use is out (P06). The text does not say who authorizes, so P06 fits only partly.
units.anchor: accessing or using AI tools without authorization
units.frag_start: accessing or using AI tools
units.fit_note: Does not say what applies when a syllabus is silent or who grants authorization.

units.why: Item [3] makes 'failure to acknowledge AI-generated contributions' itself a violation, which is P28 (nondisclosure is the violation). I chose P28 over P24 because the unit names failure to disclose as the offence, not a duty to disclose.
units.anchor: failure to acknowledge AI-generated contributions to an assignment or other academic work
units.frag_start: failure to acknowledge AI-generated contributions

units.why: The procedure says the faculty member 'must provide the associate dean with a copy of the written "Course AI Policy"' that was violated. This is a required reporting step (P81). It also presumes a written course AI policy exists, but does not require one, so P09 is not assigned.
units.anchor: must provide the associate dean with a copy of the written “Course AI Policy”
units.frag_start: If the violation involved the misuse
units.fit_note: Also implies instructors have a written Course AI Policy, without requiring one.

units.why: The levels section says Level 1 'Penalties are educative rather than punitive', for unintentional first offences. It applies to all violations including AI misuse, and it is the educative response in P68.
units.anchor: Penalties are educative rather than punitive
units.frag_start: Level 1 violations may occur because
units.frag_end: community service for a specified number of hours.
units.fit_note: General penalty scale for all integrity violations; AI is not mentioned in this passage.

units.why: Levels 2 to 4 list penalties such as 'assigning a failing grade in the course', dismissal, and revocation of a degree, tied to seriousness and intent. They apply to all integrity violations including AI misuse, which is P37 (concrete penalties in advance).
units.anchor: assigning a failing grade in the course
units.frag_start: Level 2 violations are of a more serious nature
units.policy: Penalties for integrity violations range from educative measures at Level 1 to failing the course, suspension, dismissal, transcript notation and degree revocation at Levels 2 to 4.
units.fit_note: Penalty scale covers all integrity violations; it is not specific to AI.

units.why: The sentence sets the factors for choosing a penalty: 'knowledge-level and experience', 'degree of intention', and whether this is a first offense. This is closest to P37 on penalties; P69 (evidence standards) is about proof, not penalty.
units.anchor: consideration should be given to the knowledge-level and experience of the person
units.frag_start: In determining the appropriate penalty
units.fit_note: Gives factors for choosing a penalty rather than a fixed penalty.

units.why: The faculty member is told to 'Meet with the student to discuss the incident' and determine whether a violation likely occurred before reporting. That is talking with the student before escalating (P57).
units.anchor: Meet with the student to discuss the incident and to determine the likelihood
units.frag_start: The faculty member will

units.why: The faculty member must 'Gather and preserve any relevant evidence' and document the incident. This is a procedural step in handling suspected misuse (P81), not a statement of the evidence standard (P69).
units.anchor: Gather and preserve any relevant evidence
units.frag_start: Gather and preserve any relevant
units.frag_end: document the incident and the evidence as soon as possible.

units.why: Faculty must report likely violations to the associate dean 'with a short memorandum describing the incident, the evidence and the recommended penalty'. A required report to a central office is P81.
units.anchor: must report the violation to his or her associate dean
units.frag_start: If the faculty member determines that a violation

units.why: The associate dean, after separate conversations, 'will determine if an integrity violation has occurred' and sets the penalty. This names who decides, so P80 (who enforces); sanctions are left to this officer, not the instructor.
units.anchor: the associate dean will determine if an integrity violation has occurred
units.frag_start: After separate conversations with the faculty member

units.why: 'Any person who believes that there has been a violation' should report to a faculty member or associate dean: a channel for reporting misconduct by others, P71. The line is general and does not mention AI.
units.anchor: should report it to an appropriate faculty member or associate dean
units.frag_start: Any person who believes that there has been
units.fit_note: General integrity reporting channel, not AI-specific.

units.why: Accused individuals have 'the right to notice of the specific charges, a fair consideration of the charges, a fair review of the evidence'. This is the right to a fair process that P64 describes, although it is not specific to AI.
units.anchor: right to notice of the specific charges, a fair consideration of the charges
units.frag_start: All individuals accused of a violation
units.fit_note: Due-process rights for all integrity cases; AI is not named.

units.why: Students 'may appeal the decision of the associate dean in writing to the associate provost' on three grounds. An appeal route is part of the right to respond to allegations (P64).
units.anchor: Students may appeal the decision of the associate dean in writing
units.frag_start: Students may appeal the decision of the associate dean
units.frag_end: decision of the associate provost is final.
units.fit_note: Appeal after a finding, not the right to respond during the case; not AI-specific.

units.why: 'Students should consult directly with their teachers' tells students to ask instructors about what is acceptable; the passage covers AI misuse as one example. This is P10, with a partial fit because AI is not named here.
units.anchor: Students should consult directly with their teachers.
units.frag_start: Violations of academic integrity include cheating
units.fit_note: General advice for all integrity examples; not specific to AI.

units.why: The code says everyone is responsible for 'reporting breaches to the appropriate authorities' and for confronting those who commit them. This general duty covers AI breaches as part of integrity; P71 is the nearest type.
units.anchor: for reporting breaches to the appropriate authorities
units.frag_start: each person is responsible for encouraging academic integrity
units.fit_note: General duty to confront and report breaches; AI not named.

notes: Single university-layer document; AI appears in one paragraph plus one procedural sentence, so many units are general integrity procedures that apply to AI misuse and are marked in fit_note as not AI-specific. No school or computing policy found per the collect file.
